content:
Last updated: 2026-02-10 (Vanessa)

Purpose
- Fleet/Capacity team working notes to help on-call quickly map capacity/fleet symptoms → incident taxonomy categories (v1) and pick the standard mitigations.
- This doc is intentionally a little “ops-y” (signals + what to do). Definitions live in Confluence taxonomy doc.

Scope
- Capacity/fleet shortage
- Provisioning/autoscaling lag
- Regional constraints + failover interactions
- 429/throttling vs true shortage
- Queueing and overload behavior that is primarily capacity-driven

Non-goals
- Full root cause analysis framework (belongs in postmortem)
- Per-model performance debugging (runtime doc)

---

Taxonomy mapping cheat sheet (capacity-related)

Top-level taxonomy types we expect to use most:
1) Capacity/Fleet Shortage
2) Availability/Overload (capacity-driven)
3) Routing/Fallback Misbehavior (capacity-triggered but routing is wrong)
4) Control Plane Outage (capacity was a symptom, but not the cause)
5) Telemetry/Metrics Blind Spot (we can’t prove shortage)

Fleet-owned subtypes (proposed v1 wording; match exact strings in incident-bot dropdown)
A. Capacity/Fleet Shortage
  A1. Regional capacity exhaustion
  A2. GPU pool saturation (global) / high utilization
  A3. Dedicated pool saturation / noisy-neighbor guardrails tripping
  A4. Provisioning capacity blocked (cloud quota / procurement)
  A5. Spot/preemptions causing capacity drop

B. Capacity/Provisioning Lag
  B1. Cluster autoscaler lag (nodes pending too long)
  B2. GPU provisioning lag (image pull, driver init, node readiness)
  B3. Warm pool depleted / cold-start storm

C. Quota/Throttling (NOT always capacity)
  C1. Customer quota enforcement (expected throttles)
  C2. Burst policy enforcement (Dedicated)
  C3. Internal safety valve throttling (protecting fleet)

Notes on boundaries
- If routing is correctly falling back (expected behavior) but customers see model/region changes + latency, this is still a capacity incident (Fleet) with “routing fallback triggered by capacity” as a contributing factor (not primary).
- If routing fails to fall back, falls back to an incompatible tier, or amplifies impact (e.g., retries storm), primary becomes Routing/Fallback Misbehavior (Routing owns), with capacity as contributing.
- If customers see 429s but overall GPU headroom exists, likely Quota/Throttling (check rate limiter dashboards + customer config) rather than capacity.

---

Signals: what to look at (and what it means)

1) GPU saturation / pool health
Primary signals
- GPU utilization (avg + p95) by pool (hosted shared, dedicated, private)
  - Thresholds we use in practice:
    - Sustained >85% for 10–15m across a pool + rising queue wait = “saturation likely impacting latency/errors”.
    - Spiky >95% without queueing can be OK; look for queue wait + request timeouts.
- GPU memory pressure / OOM rate
  - High OOM can masquerade as “capacity” but is often runtime regression or model config. If OOM spikes coincide with rollout/version change, consider Runtime Regression primary.
- Scheduler queue wait (time from admission → execution)
  - Strong signal for “insufficient effective capacity” even when utilization looks flat.
- Request admission rejects / overload shedder events

Secondary signals
- KV cache hit rate / prefix cache hit rate
  - Decreasing cache hit rate increases effective compute demand; can trigger saturation.
- Batch size distribution changes
  - Sudden drop in batch size = throughput loss, may look like shortage.

Interpretation tips
- High utilization with stable p95 latency = acceptable steady-state.
- Rising queue wait + rising p95/p99 latency = shortage or provisioning lag.
- Rising 5xx/timeouts with flat utilization can mean control plane, networking, or runtime stalls.

2) Provisioning / autoscaling lag
Primary signals
- Pending GPU nodes (requested vs ready)
- Time-to-ready histogram for new GPU nodes
- Cluster autoscaler events: scale-up requested, scale-up blocked reasons
- Image pull/driver init failures on new nodes
- Warm pool size and depletion rate

Common failure modes
- Cold-start storm: sudden traffic ramp drains warm pool; autoscaling can’t catch up.
- Node readiness gating: driver/cuda initialization or host OS updates increase readiness time.
- Quota/procurement blocked: cloud quota, reserved capacity ceiling, or procurement delay.

Interpretation tips
- If pending nodes exist but readiness time is high, classify as Capacity/Provisioning Lag (Fleet) vs pure shortage.
- If autoscaler is blocked due to quota, classify as Capacity/Fleet Shortage → “Provisioning capacity blocked (cloud quota/procurement)”.

3) Regional constraints / failover interactions
Primary signals
- Regional pool utilization/queue wait divergence (region A red, region B green)
- Routing fallback_reason=capacity events (from router metrics)
- Regional admission rejects / overload shed
- Cloud provider status + AZ-level capacity notes (if we have them)

Common failure modes
- Single-region exhaustion due to uneven demand or hardware skew.
- Failover amplifies load into an already hot region.
- Regional GPU supply constraints (can’t scale within region even if global inventory exists).

Interpretation tips
- If region A is saturated and router is failing over correctly, primary is capacity (regional capacity exhaustion).
- If failover is triggered but routes to the wrong tier/region or creates retry storms, primary can be routing.

4) 429 / throttling vs true capacity
Primary signals
- Rate limiter / quota enforcement counters (by customer, by key, by route)
- Dedicated burst policy counters (burst window, max concurrency)
- “Safety valve” throttles (fleet protection)

Interpretation tips
- 429s with normal queue wait and healthy utilization often means quota/policy.
- 429s + high queue wait + high utilization often means the system is shedding load due to shortage; still classify as capacity-driven overload.

---

Incident type selection guide (what should the IC pick?)

If the symptom is primarily…

A) p95 latency rising + queue wait rising + utilization high
- Primary: Capacity/Fleet Shortage (or Availability/Overload if errors dominate)
- Subtype guess:
  - If localized: Regional capacity exhaustion
  - If fleet-wide: GPU pool saturation
- Owners:
  - Primary: Infra/Fleet
  - Consulted: Routing (for traffic shifting), Runtime (if perf anomaly), Observability (if signal gaps)

B) Elevated 5xx / timeouts + overload shed events + utilization high
- Primary: Availability/Overload (capacity-driven)
- Contributing: Capacity/Fleet Shortage
- Owners:
  - Primary: SRE (incident mgmt) + Infra/Fleet for mitigation

C) Degradation begins right after failover or router policy change
- If fallback_reason=capacity and behavior is expected: Capacity/Fleet Shortage (regional)
- If fallback behavior is wrong/unexpected: Routing/Fallback Misbehavior (Routing primary)

D) Latency/5xx but dashboards show “unknown” due to missing metrics
- Primary: Telemetry/Metrics Blind Spot (until proven otherwise)
- Action: engage Observability early; do not assume capacity without queue/util signals

E) Sudden 429 spike for one customer during “burst”
- Primary: Quota/Throttling (Dedicated burst policy) unless fleet signals show saturation

---

Standard mitigations (Fleet playbook snippets)

Mitigation ladder (try in this order; pick the smallest lever that stabilizes)

1) Reduce demand (fastest)
- Enable/verify graceful degradation policy:
  - Lower max_tokens or cap output length for affected routes (if policy exists)
  - Prefer fallback model variants with similar quality but lower cost
  - Tighten concurrency per customer (Dedicated) if one tenant is spiking
- Turn on or increase batching within SLO constraints
- Temporarily disable optional features that inflate compute (rerankers, long-context routes) if we have kill-switches

2) Shift demand (fast)
- Rebalance traffic across regions if healthy capacity exists elsewhere
- For Dedicated: move traffic to secondary pool (if contracted) or temporarily borrow burst capacity per policy
- Validate router is emitting fallback_reason=capacity correctly (helps classification and later reporting)

3) Increase supply (slower)
- Trigger manual scale-up of GPU node pools
- Allocate emergency capacity from reserve / warm pool
- Expedite instance acquisition or lift quota (cloud provider / procurement)

4) Stabilize the system (when things are chaotic)
- Increase admission control aggressiveness to protect tail latency (avoid death spiral)
- Reduce retry storms:
  - Confirm client retry guidance is being honored
  - If router is retrying internally, reduce retries/timeouts temporarily

Customer tier notes
- Hosted: prioritize global stability; prefer demand shaping + regional rebalance.
- Dedicated: be explicit about what is policy vs incident. If customer is hitting their burst guardrails, classify as Quota/Throttling unless fleet is impacted.
- Private: most “capacity” symptoms are actually customer-side capacity/cluster; route to Private Deployments/Networking SME and ensure classification reflects “private connectivity/config” unless we control the fleet.

---

Suggested dashboards / queries (names are approximate; link in incident-bot once wired)

Fleet capacity
- GPU pool utilization by tier/region
- Queue wait + scheduler backlog by pool
- Admission rejects / overload shed rate
- Node scale-up requested vs ready (autoscaling health)

Routing correlation
- fallback_reason breakdown (capacity/health/policy/timeout)
- % requests served by fallback model/region (to quantify degradation)

Customer focus
- Top N customers by concurrency / token rate
- Dedicated pool saturation by customer (if allowed)

---

Ownership + escalation notes (for the taxonomy program)

Capacity/Fleet Shortage (all subtypes)
- Primary: Infra/Fleet (Vanessa / on-call)
- Secondary/consulted:
  - Routing: traffic shift + policy safety valves
  - SRE: incident command + comms
  - Observability: validate signals + metric gaps
  - Runtime: if suspected throughput regression vs true shortage

Routing/Fallback Misbehavior (capacity-triggered)
- Primary: Routing
- Fleet consulted: confirm capacity state, provide safe shift targets

Quota/Throttling
- Primary:
  - Hosted quota: Platform/Control Plane (rate limits/config)
  - Dedicated burst policy: Dedicated Platform (with Fleet consult)
- Fleet consulted: confirm not a broader capacity event

---

Examples from recent incidents (for training/backfill)

1) “Intermittent 500s during region failover”
- Pattern: region A saturated → failover to region B → mixed 500s/latency
- What mattered: queue wait spiked in both regions after failover; fallback_reason=capacity was high.
- Classification guidance:
  - If failover behaved as designed: Capacity/Fleet Shortage → Regional capacity exhaustion
  - If failover routing looped / wrong tier: Routing/Fallback Misbehavior

2) “Dedicated customer sees 429s during burst window”
- Pattern: single customer; overall dedicated pool utilization normal; policy counters high.
- Classification: Quota/Throttling → Dedicated burst policy enforcement

3) “Cold-start storm after warm pool depletion”
- Pattern: traffic ramp drains warm pool; pending nodes; time-to-ready 18–25m.
- Classification: Capacity/Provisioning Lag → Warm pool depleted / GPU provisioning lag

---

Open questions / parking lot
- Do we want a separate subtype for “capacity loss due to perf regression” (e.g., throughput drops 20% with same load) or always treat as Runtime Regression primary?
- Where do we classify “cloud provider AZ capacity failures” when we can’t provision but demand is normal? (Probably Capacity/Fleet Shortage → Provisioning capacity blocked.)
- Dedicated: clarify boundary between “policy expected” vs “incident” when customers are contractually entitled to burst. Need alignment with Product + SLA matrix.
